# EUA: pedidos de auxílio-desemprego surpreendem para baixo, déficit comercial se amplia e corte na projeção de PIB do 1º tri para +2,9%

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** Dados semanais de emprego e balança comercial dos EUA  
**General comment:** Leitura mista e marginalmente negativa para o crescimento — mercado de trabalho firme, mas detalhes do comércio levam a revisão para baixo do PIB

### Contexto
Comentário publicado logo após a divulgação dos pedidos iniciais de auxílio-desemprego (semana encerrada em 28 de março) e da balança comercial de fevereiro, usado para atualizar o rastreamento do PIB do 1º trimestre.

### Os argumentos
- **O mercado de trabalho segue firme.** Os pedidos iniciais caíram 9k, para 202k, contrariando a expectativa de consenso de leve alta e ficando abaixo tanto da estimativa do [REDACTED] (205k) quanto da mediana (212k). A média móvel de quatro semanas recuou 3k, para 208k. No detalhe estadual, houve alta de 2k no Texas e quedas em Michigan (-4k, revertendo parte do salto de 6k da semana anterior) e Iowa (-2k). Os pedidos continuados subiram 25k, para 1.841k, praticamente em linha com o consenso.

- **O déficit comercial se ampliou, mas o número cheio esconde a piora subjacente.** O déficit aumentou US$ 2,6 bi, para US$ 57,3 bi, ficando abaixo do consenso (US$ 60,6 bi). As importações de bens subiram US$ 14,0 bi, puxadas por produtos eletrônicos, computadores, semicondutores e metais não ferrosos — provável reflexo do investimento ligado a IA. As exportações de bens cresceram US$ 11,5 bi, mas em grande parte por conta de ouro, que não entra nas estatísticas de PIB. Excluindo ouro, o déficit foi bem maior — US$ 79,5 bi, ante US$ 68,0 bi em janeiro — o que representa uma deterioração real de US$ 10,5 bi no mês.

- **Os detalhes do comércio ficaram mais fracos do que o pressuposto no rastreamento.** Como o ouro infla o número cheio sem contrapartida no PIB, a piora relevante é a medida ex-ouro, mais fraca que as premissas anteriores. Isso motivou o corte da projeção.

### Implicações
- A estimativa de rastreamento do PIB do 1º trimestre foi reduzida em 0,3pp, para +2,9% (trimestral anualizado).
- A estimativa de vendas finais domésticas privadas do 1º trimestre está em +2,1%, sinalizando que a demanda interna subjacente segue mais moderada que o crescimento total.

# US Data: Firm Retail Sales and a Manufacturing Surprise Lift Q2 GDP Tracking to +2.4%

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US June retail sales, Philly Fed, jobless claims  
**General comment:** Constructive read of the data; incrementally raises Q2 growth tracking, broadly in line with a solid-activity consensus.

### Context
A same-day comment on the June retail sales release alongside the July Philadelphia Fed manufacturing survey and weekly jobless claims, feeding into the Q2 GDP tracking picture.

### The case
- **Consumer spending held up in June and prior months were revised higher.** Core retail sales (ex-autos, gas and building materials) rose 0.5%, matching consensus, with the May level revised up 0.2% on small upward revisions to both April and May. Strength was concentrated in nonstore retailers (+1.9%) and sporting goods (+1.3%), while health and personal care fell (-0.8%). Headline sales rose only 0.2%, held back by a 5.3% drop in gasoline spending, but the May level was revised up 0.4%. On the PCE and CPI details, real core retail sales are estimated to have grown at a 7.1% three-month annualized pace through June.
- **The Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index jumped to its strongest level since November 2021.** The headline rose 31.1 points to +41.4, far above the +12.5 consensus, and the internals were broadly firm: new orders, shipments and employment all rose. Both prices-paid and prices-received measures increased. The one soft spot was the forward-looking six-months-ahead business conditions index, which fell 15.8 points to +34.4.
- **Jobless claims point to a still-tight labor market.** Initial claims fell 8k to 208k, below expectations, with the four-week average down to 214k. State-level moves largely reversed Independence Day–related increases. Continuing claims declined 16k to 1,805k.

### Implications
- The firmer-than-assumed retail details lifted the Q2 GDP tracking estimate by 0.2pp to +2.4% quarter-over-quarter annualized, with domestic final sales at +2.3%.
- Together the releases depict resilient activity — solid consumption, a manufacturing upside surprise and low claims — though the drop in the Philly Fed's forward expectations tempers the read on momentum ahead.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Supply Risks Return

# Oil Shock Flips Rates to Hawkish, but Weak Labor Data Caps the Move

**Theme:** How rates markets should trade an energy supply shock against a softening growth backdrop, across the US, Europe and Australia
**Markets:** Developed-market rates
**Source:** [REDACTED] (George Cole), 6 March 2026

### Definitive impacts
- Terminal-rate pricing re-rallied modestly on Friday after a softer US jobs report, though the front-end response to the downside surprise was muted; greens and blues remain firmly richer and the broader curve flattening from February is largely intact.
- Parts of the forward curve hit hardest by the oil-led selloff (e.g. H7, M7) are roughly unchanged over the last month.
- The EUR front-end now prices ECB hikes in 2026, with the risk skew shifting from cuts to hikes — a repricing larger than in early December.
- The GBP front-end has priced out almost all 2026 cuts, moving toward the upside-risk scenarios [REDACTED] economists had outlined.
- Rates carry has flattened to negative over the past month: vol-selling returns are flat-to-negative and swap spreads have tightened across the curve, with long-end-led underperformance most pronounced.
- US rates market function remains orderly: market depth has thinned (typical as vol rises), but price-impact of orderflow, curve dispersion and funding costs are stable.
- [REDACTED] commodities team raised baseline energy price forecasts to roughly 10% above pre-conflict levels.
- [REDACTED] economists lifted the probability of an RBA March hike to 40%, above the market-implied ~25%.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] expects Friday's re-rally in US terminal pricing to extend, arguing weak labor demand should moderate the hawkish impulse from higher energy; if markets read further oil upside as a growth threat, the beaten-down front-end forwards (H7, M7) should turn supportive.
- [REDACTED] would lean against rallies in the US inflation curve: adjusting for the energy move, inflation forwards have lagged their usual oil relationship (signalling embedded growth downside), yet the 1-to-2y implied inflation landing zone still sits above the economists' forecast.
- [REDACTED] favors positively-carrying, level-insulated trades — 5s7s steepeners or 15-20y vs 30s longs — over outright longs, given the risk overhang despite improved valuations.
- [REDACTED] sees ECB pricing as not having overshot: baseline is no ECB hikes through 2026 (contingent on only temporary disruption), but higher energy reduces the odds of cuts, and a larger shock raises core-inflation spillover and hike risk.
- [REDACTED] sees UK rates as asymmetric toward lower 10y/30y Gilt yields on any Middle East de-escalation; end-year 10y Gilt forecast is 4.0% with clear upside risks. Relative to the ECB, [REDACTED] sees more room for UK rates to retrace lower because ECB cuts are unlikely.
- [REDACTED] expects the Riksbank and Norges Bank to hold next week, seeing option value in waiting; SEK/NOK repricing is not clearly excessive, and in NOK higher energy is a positive growth impulse via terms of trade. Swiss hike risk stays low given currency strength.
- [REDACTED] sees AUD risk as hawkish near-term (front-end skewed bearish, March hike underpriced) but dovish medium-term: further-dated forwards sit above the economists' terminal view and look too cheap, with normalization cuts expected in 2027.

### Backdrop
Through February, rates markets traded growth downside, driven by AI-disruption concerns, which had revived the hedge value of duration and compressed inflation forwards. An energy shock tied to conflict in the Middle East (strikes on Iran) then reintroduced supply-side volatility, abruptly shifting the market's dominant trading dimension from growth to inflation. Central banks enter this with differing starting points: the ECB and BoE had been expected to ease in 2026, the RBA was near the end of a hiking cycle, and the Scandinavian and Swiss central banks face energy shocks that hit their economies asymmetrically.

### At issue
The note assesses how DM rates should trade the renewed oil shock now colliding with fresh signs of labor-market weakness. Two concurrent developments frame it: (1) energy prices spiked alongside the conflict, prompting a swift hawkish repricing in US, European and UK front-ends; and (2) Friday's US jobs report surprised to the downside, reviving concerns that labor demand is too weak to sustain a stable labor market. The inflation curve's response looks consistent with a permanent level shift in energy rather than a temporary spike. Regional meetings next week (Riksbank, Norges Bank) and RBA commentary sharpen the near-term policy-response questions.

### Unpacked
The central tension is that a supply shock and a demand-side softening are pushing rates in opposite directions at the same time. **The oil shock handed inflation-upside risks the upper hand over growth fears, but the muted front-end reaction to a weak jobs print signals that the prevailing macro backdrop should temper how far the hawkish trade can run.** The call is that markets have not yet fully absorbed higher energy as a reason to worry about growth — and when they do, the forwards most damaged by the selloff should recover.

In the US, valuations have improved the case for outright longs, but the two-sided risk — hawkish energy pressure versus latent growth downside — argues against directional exposure. **[REDACTED] prefers structures that earn positive carry while insulating against further level shifts, since both the vol backdrop and the shift toward hawkish policy have turned carry itself into a headwind.** Fiscal supply is not yet a focal point, but an extended conflict could reintroduce it as a fresh risk source, which is where the note's "supply risks return" framing bites.

In Europe, the read is that the aggressive repricing to ECB hikes has not overshot given genuine commodity risk, even if long-rate/short-vol positioning exacerbated the move. **The key nuance is asymmetry: with the downside distribution of yields limited, upside energy scenarios can justify a premium against hikes, and a larger shock raises the odds that hikes actually become necessary through core spillovers.** The UK sits differently — the same vol shock priced out cuts, but because a temporary disruption is the base case, the distribution skews toward lower Gilt yields on de-escalation, making UK rates the cleaner retracement candidate versus a less flexible ECB. Scandinavia is a live test of how central banks respond to energy shocks, complicated by Norway's positive terms-of-trade impulse.

**In Australia, the near-term and medium-term skews point opposite ways: front-end risk is modestly hawkish on RBA commentary and a higher-probability March hike, but further-out forwards sit too cheap relative to a benign underlying inflation and productivity picture.** [REDACTED] expects decelerating inflation to permit normalization cuts in 2027, so the medium-term risk is toward a flatter front-end, back toward pre-oil-spike levels.

The note lists trade recommendations across curve and carry structures but frames the actionable stance around relative-value and spread trades rather than a single outright directional idea.

# Global Week Ahead: Four EM/DM Cuts Priced In, [REDACTED] Splits From Consensus on US Growth and Japan Inflation

**Theme:** Central bank week plus a batch of top-tier inflation and activity prints, with several notable [REDACTED]-vs-consensus gaps  
**Markets:** Global rates and macro data  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 15 February 2026

### Landscape
- Four central banks meet, with [REDACTED] in line with consensus on all: Philippines to 4.25% (from 4.5%), New Zealand to 2.25% (from 2.5%), Indonesia held at 4.75%, and Romania held at 6.5%.
- Key global releases due include Japan Core CPI, Euro Area Manufacturing and Services PMIs, US PCE, South Africa CPI and UK Core CPI.
- [REDACTED] sits above consensus on Euro Area Services PMI (51.9 vs 51.8, last 51.6) and US December core PCE mom (0.37% vs 0.3%, last 0.2%).
- [REDACTED] sits below consensus on US GDP QoQ (1.6% vs 3.0%, last 4.4%), Japan New Core CPI yoy (2.6% vs 2.7%, last 2.9%) and South Africa CPI yoy (3.4% vs 3.5%, last 3.6%).

### Drivers
- US inflation and growth pull in opposite directions in the [REDACTED] view: a firmer core PCE (0.37% mom) alongside a materially softer GDP read (1.6% vs 3.0% consensus) — the growth gap is the larger deviation.
- Japan disinflation is the recurring theme, with [REDACTED] below consensus across Core CPI (2.6%), New Core CPI (2.6%) and CPI ex. fresh food (1.9% vs 2.0%, last 2.4%) — all pointing lower than prior prints.
- Japan trade is the sharpest out-of-consensus cluster: imports seen far stronger (7.0% yoy vs 3.2%) and the trade balance far more negative (−¥2,510bn vs −¥2,142bn, versus a small surplus last).
- Euro Area activity edges up in the [REDACTED] read, with France Services PMI called at 49.4 (vs 48.9 consensus, 48.4 last) — still sub-50 but improving.

### Unpacked
This is a calendar-and-forecast note, not an argument; its content is the map of what prints next week and where [REDACTED]'s economists diverge from the street. **The four scheduled central bank decisions carry no [REDACTED] surprise — forecasts match consensus at every meeting, with cuts expected in the Philippines and New Zealand and holds in Indonesia and Romania.** The interest is therefore in the data, not the policy calendar.

**On the US, [REDACTED] pairs a hotter core PCE with a much cooler GDP figure, a 1.6% versus 3.0% consensus gap on growth that is the note's single largest deviation among the key global indicators.** The two together sketch a stagflation-leaning tilt in the [REDACTED] numbers relative to the street, though the note frames them only as forecast differences, not a scenario call.

**Japan is where [REDACTED] is most consistently and most sharply off consensus**, running below the street on every inflation measure listed while flagging an outsized trade deterioration — imports at 7.0% against 3.2% consensus and a trade balance near −¥2.5tn where last month showed a small surplus. The disinflation and the widening import bill are the flagged themes for the week in that market.

The note carries no explicit trade idea and flags no risks; it is a forecast scoreboard, with directional gaps to consensus doing the work. The out-of-consensus items — France Services PMI, Japan imports and trade balance, Japan CPI ex. fresh food, and South Africa core CPI (3.2% vs 3.3%) — are those exceeding one standard deviation of historical surprise.

# Semana à Frente: Payrolls Fracos e ISM na Linha de 50 Ancoram uma Agenda de Dados Densa

**Theme:** [REDACTED] forecasts vs. consensus for the week's central bank decisions and data  
**Markets:** Global macro (rates, activity, inflation)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 31 Aug 2025

### Landscape
- Poland's policy rate seen cut to 4.75% from 5.0%, in line with consensus.
- Malaysia's rate seen held at 2.75%, in line with consensus and unchanged from last.
- US ISM Manufacturing forecast at 50.0 (consensus 49.0, last 48.0) — [REDACTED] above consensus and back to the expansion threshold.

# G10 Consumers: Solid Balance Sheets, but Energy Costs Bite Into Real Incomes

**Theme:** Spending edges up while higher energy prices erode real incomes in North America and Western Europe  
**Markets:** G10 household consumer health  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 30 July 2026  

### Landscape
- Consumer health proxy stands around P70 in Japan, ~P50 in the Euro area and Australia, ~P40 in the US and Canada, and ~P35 in the UK — improving in Japan, the US and Canada since the last update, slightly worse in the Euro area and UK.
- Household net worth to income sits near all-time highs in Japan and Australia, ~P95 in the US, ~P90 in Canada and the Euro area, and ~P55 in the UK.
- Real income growth is subdued at P10 in the US, P25 in the UK and Canada and P40 in the Euro area, but firmer in Australia (P75) and Japan (P95) where price controls have cushioned the energy shock.
- US real spending rose 0.4% in June, a 2.5% six-month annualized pace; spending-growth percentiles improved in Japan (P85), the Euro area (P65), Canada (P55) and the US (P35), and held at P25 in Australia.
- Unemployment is near historical lows in the Euro area (6.3%), Japan (2.5%) and Australia (4.4%), around P70 in the US (4.2%), P50 in Canada (6.5%) and P30 in the UK (4.9% 3mma).
- Debt service ratios are low by history in the US (P75) and Euro area (P65), average in Japan (P50), and heavier in Canada (P20), Australia (P35) and the UK (P45).

### Drivers
- Higher energy prices are the dominant fresh drag, eroding real incomes in North America and Western Europe; government price-control measures in Japan and Australia have limited the hit there.
- Consumer sentiment is recovering off low levels across DMs on earlier lower energy prices — US UMich rose to 54.4 in July (from 49.5) and Australia to 83.9 (from 80.6, still 17% below its historical average) — but the rebound predates the July 7 resumption of US strikes on Iran and the subsequent gas-price rise.
- US spending is being propped up temporarily by OBBBA-related tax cuts and World Cup–related spending, tailwinds expected to fade.
- Wage growth is cooling at the margin: Japan basic wage growth slowed to 3.0% in May (from 3.3%) but stays elevated; UK private-sector regular pay held at 2.9% y/y in May.
- Labor markets remain a support in the Euro area, Australia and Japan, but stay notably weaker in the UK.
- Canadian house prices show signs of stabilizing after falling since 2022; mortgage debt growth runs above trend in Japan and Australia, while credit growth is near average in Western Europe and edged down in North America.

### Risks
- Downside (US): spending growth is expected to slow to just 1.5% Q4/Q4 in 2026 as higher energy costs weigh on real incomes and the tax-cut and World Cup boosts unwind.
- Downside (Australia): the economics team anticipates deteriorating spending on lower house prices and soft real income growth.
- Sentiment readings likely overstate current confidence: over 70% of US survey interviews were completed before the July 7 escalation and gas-price increase, so the July rebound may not hold.

### Unpacked
The dashboard's central message is a split between stocks and flows. **Balance sheets remain a genuine source of strength across the G10, but that cushion is being tested by an income squeeze concentrated in North America and Western Europe.** Net-worth-to-income ratios sit near or above the 90th percentile almost everywhere except the UK, yet real net worth *growth* has slowed — to P30 in the Euro area — and is only middling elsewhere (P90 Japan, P55 US and Australia, P35 Canada, P30 UK).

The energy shock is the organizing theme. **Where governments have intervened on prices — Japan and Australia — real income growth stays firm (P95 and P75); where they have not, it is weak (P10 in the US, P25 in the UK and Canada).** The US figure is flagged as exaggerated by policy-induced swings and lower immigration, so the underlying deterioration is somewhat less severe than the headline percentile implies.

Spending has so far held up better than incomes, but the report is explicit that this is partly borrowed from the future. **US real spending's resilient 2.5% six-month pace rests in part on OBBBA tax cuts and World Cup spending, and is expected to decelerate to 1.5% on a Q4/Q4 basis in 2026.** The saving rate edged down further in the US in June while remaining elevated in Western Europe, Canada and Australia — leaving those consumers more buffer but also signaling more caution.

The sentiment recovery deserves a caveat that the report itself supplies. **Confidence rebounded on lower energy prices, but the surveys largely closed before the July 7 escalation with Iran and the ensuing rise in gas prices, so the improvement may already be stale.** Relief was sharpest among low-income consumers, who are also most exposed if energy costs climb again.

On the financial side, the picture is uneven by region. Debt service burdens are comfortable in the US and Euro area but elevated in Canada and Australia, where interest expenses remain high. Canada offers a tentative bright spot: house prices show signs of stabilizing after a multi-year decline, though real income growth there has deteriorated and confidence stays weak. No explicit trade idea is offered — this is a monitoring report, and its scoreboard is the deliverable.

subject: G10 Consumer Dashboard: June 2026: Resilience in Japan
summary:
# G10 Consumer Dashboard: Balance Sheets Hold, but Energy Costs Set to Bite in H2

**Theme:** Strong household wealth colliding with an energy-driven real-income squeeze; Japan the standout  
**Markets:** G10 consumers  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 1 July 2026  

### Landscape
- Household net worth relative to income sits near all-time highs in the US, Japan and Australia, around P90 in Canada and the Euro area, and around P55 in the UK.
- The US saving rate held at 3.0% in May after three straight monthly declines, and remains elevated across DMs outside Japan.
- US consumer sentiment (UMich) rose to 48.9 in June from 44.8 in May, driven by a 2.6pt gain in current conditions; Australian sentiment fell 2.9% mom to 80.6.
- Unemployment is near historical lows in the Euro area (6.3%), Japan (2.5%) and Australia (4.4%), around P65 in the US (4.3%), P35 in the UK (4.9% 3mma) and P20 in Canada (6.6%).
- Debt service ratios are low by history in the US (P75) and Euro area (P65), average in Japan (P50), but heavier in Canada (P20), Australia (P35) and the UK (P45).
- The overall consumer-health proxy stands near P55 in Japan and the Euro area, ~P50 in Australia, ~P40 in the US and UK, and ~P30 in Canada.

### Drivers
- Real income growth is the central drag: below historical averages in the US and Canada, at P15 in Australia, P35 in the UK and P40 in the Euro area, pushed down by higher energy prices — with the European hit expected to be more backloaded given greater gas and electricity exposure and slower pass-through.
- Japan runs against the grain — real income growth at P90, basic wage growth steady at an elevated 3.4% and real wages positive for a fourth straight month, aided by government price-control measures cushioning the energy shock.
- Spending is still resilient but diverging: real spending growth improved in Japan (P80), the UK (P65), Canada (P50), the Euro area (P45) and Australia (P25), while slowing in the US (P15); US real personal spending rose 0.3% mom in May.
- Labor markets are splitting — tight in the Euro area, Australia and Japan, normalized in the US, and notably softer in the UK and Canada, with UK private-sector pay growth easing to 2.9% in April.
- Housing and credit are mixed: Canadian house prices are still falling but show signs of stabilizing, mortgage debt growth runs above trend in Japan and Australia, and US household credit growth ticked up.

### Risks
- Downside: the energy shock is expected to erode real incomes further, with [REDACTED] projecting US year-over-year spending growth to slow from 2.1% to 1.3% by year-end and the saving rate to normalize — the risk being weaker H2 consumption than current resilience implies.
- Downside (Europe-specific): [REDACTED] flags natural gas and electricity prices rising further in coming months and passing through gradually to consumer prices, making the European income hit larger and later than elsewhere.
- Downside (Australia): house price expectations dropped 14.9% mom, led by Sydney (-19%) and Melbourne (-18%) where prices are already falling, pointing to weakening wealth perceptions.

### Unpacked
The core tension is between stock and flow. **Balance sheets remain a genuine source of strength across the G10, but that cushion is being drawn down by an income squeeze that [REDACTED] expects to intensify into the second half.** Real net worth growth since the last update improved in Japan (P90), the Euro area (P60) and Australia (P45) but slowed in the US (P55), Canada (P35) and the UK (P25) — the wealth backdrop is still favorable but no longer uniformly improving.

**Japan is the report's clear outlier, and the reason for its title: tight labor market, high net-worth-to-income, real wages positive for four months running, and spending growth at P80.** The government's price-control measures are explicitly credited with blunting the energy shock that is dragging on peers, leaving Japanese real incomes at P90 while most of the G10 sits below historical averages.

The sentiment rebound following the US-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was broad but shallow. In the US the improvement came from lower-income consumers, who benefited most from early-month gasoline relief given fuel's larger share of their budgets. **Australia moved the other way — sentiment fell on weak readings for family finances (-7.5% mom) and long-term economic conditions (-3.2% mom), alongside a sharp drop in house price expectations.**

The US carries the clearest deceleration signal. Spending growth has slipped to P15 even as it held positive in May, and [REDACTED] reads the recent income weakness as partly one-off distortions but also genuine softening plus an energy drag. **The forecast is explicit: US spending growth slowing to 1.3% by year-end with the saving rate normalizing as real-income headwinds bite.** Canada remains the weakest overall at ~P30, with elevated interest expenses and still-falling (though stabilizing) house prices, while the Euro area and UK carry soft-to-average health with Europe's energy hit still ahead of it.

# G10 Consumer Dashboard: Strong Balance Sheets and Jobs, but Weak Sentiment and Softening Incomes

**Theme:** Consumer health broadly stable to improving, led by UK, Canada and Australia  
**Markets:** G10 developed-market consumers  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 1 January 2026  

### Landscape
- Household net worth-to-income sits near or above P90 in the US, Australia, Euro area, Japan and Canada, and around P60 in the UK.
- Consumer sentiment remains below its historical average across all of the G10 (Exhibit 13).
- Unemployment is near historical lows in the Euro area (6.4%), Japan (2.6%) and Australia (4.3%); it stands at P55 in the US (4.6%), P45 in Canada (6.5%) and P25 in the UK (5.1%, 3mma).
- The saving rate is below its pre-pandemic level in the US but remains elevated in the other G10 economies (Exhibit 10).
- Debt service ratios are low by historical standards in the US, Euro area and Japan, but higher in Canada, Australia and the UK.
- Overall consumer-health proxy: ~P60 Australia, ~P55 Euro area, ~P50 Japan, P40 US and UK, ~P35 Canada — improved or flat everywhere since the last update.

### Drivers
- Real income growth improved in the UK (P55) and Australia (P45) but deteriorated in the US (P10), Japan (P35) and Canada (P45); UK private-sector pay slowed to 3.9% in October (from 4.2%), and Japan's nominal cash wages rose to 2.6% yoy though only 2.2% on a same-sample basis.
- Real spending growth improved in Australia (P60), the UK (P40) and Canada (P30), was flat in Japan (P40), and slowed in the US (P35) and Euro area (P35); Australia's 1.3% October jump was driven by discretionary spending on promotions and festival events.
- Labor markets diverged: unemployment fell 0.4pp in Canada but rose in the US and UK — though the US increase was ~2bp ex the rise in unemployed government workers tied to the deferred resignation program.
- Real net worth growth improved in Australia (P40), Japan (P55) and Canada (P45) but stayed at or below its historical average in the Euro area (P50), US (P45) and UK (P35).
- Housing is broadly flat across DMs but still falling in Canada; mortgage credit growth is subdued in North America and Western Europe but above pre-pandemic pace in Japan and Australia.

### Unpacked
The overall message is one of resilient fundamentals offset by soft mood. G10 consumers still draw support from healthy labor markets and strong balance sheets, but real income and net worth growth have softened and sentiment stays low. **The net improvement this month is concentrated in the UK, Canada and Australia, while the US shows the weakest income momentum in the panel.**

In the US, the sentiment picture is mixed under the surface: the UMich headline ticked up 2.3pt, yet its current-conditions component fell 0.4pt to 50.7 — a new historical low. Real personal spending was flat in September but year-over-year growth held at a solid 2.4%, and US real income growth slipped to P10, the lowest income reading across the G10. **The US remains the outlier on saving — the only economy where the saving rate sits below its pre-pandemic level.**

Australia stands out on the activity side. Spending accelerated to 1.3% in October, well above expectations, but the gain leaned on discretionary categories boosted by promotional discounting and major festival events — a composition worth discounting for durability. Sentiment there also retraced 9.0% after an unusually high November print, so the confidence signal reversed even as spending firmed.

**Canada's improvement is led by the labor market, where unemployment fell 0.4pp, even as consumer confidence stays weak and house prices keep declining.** Interest expenses remain elevated in Canada (Exhibit 15) and outstanding household debt climbed there while ticking down in the US, leaving Canadian consumers the lowest-ranked in the panel at ~P35 despite a high net-worth-to-income ratio.

The UK is the clearest weak spot on jobs: the labor market deteriorated further, with unemployment at 5.1% (3mma) ranking around P25, the softest in the group, even as real income and spending edged up. On methodology, note that from the June 2025 publication pension assets were stripped from the UK net-worth measures to harmonize with G10 peers, given their illiquidity and a persistent, outlier devaluation. **The composite weights real spending, the unemployment gap and consumer confidence at 20% each, real income at 15%, and debt-service, real net worth and net-worth-to-income at 10/10/5% — so labor and spending dominate the health scores.**

The report flags no explicit risk scenarios and offers no trade idea; it is a dashboard update, not a directional call.

subject: G10 Inflation Monitor: Core Inflation Surprises to the Downside Outside of the UK
summary:
# Core Disinflation Broadens Across G10 — the UK the Lone Holdout

**Theme:** June core inflation surprised down almost everywhere; energy collapse reshapes the forecast path  
**Markets:** G10 / DM inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Megan Peters, 30 July 2026  

### Landscape
- [REDACTED] trimmed core (monthly annualized) fell to 1.1% in the Euro area (vs. 2.6%) and 1.7% in the US (PCE forecast, vs. 2.1%), held at 1.8% in Canada, and rose to 2.2% in both Japan (vs. 1.6%) and the UK (vs. 1.8%).
- On a 3-month annualized basis, trimmed core eased to 1.9% in the US (PCE, vs. 2.3%), was flat at 2.2% in the Euro area and 1.8% in Canada, and rose in Japan (1.3%) and the UK (1.7%).
- The share of the headline basket running above 4% (six-month annualized) ticked down in the US (31%) but rose in Japan (29% vs. 18%), the UK (36% vs. 32%) and Canada (22% vs. 19%); the above-8% share kept climbing only in the US (16% vs. 15%).
- Aggregate DM surprise indices fell to -23bp for headline (vs. -1bp end-June) and -13bp for core (vs. +2bp); over 12 months the largest cumulative downside surprises are in Canada (-80bp), the UK (-43bp) and the US (-31bp).
- Traditional 3-month core has moderated from its cyclical peak by roughly 7pp in the UK, 5pp in the Euro area and Canada, and 4pp in the US.

### Drivers
- Energy pulled back sharply following the US-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz: 3-month annualized energy inflation collapsed to 7% in the US (vs. 104%), 11% in Canada (vs. 102%), 3% in the Euro area (vs. 44%), 6% in the UK (vs. 31%) and 19% in Japan (vs. 41%).
- US core goods turned outright deflationary (-0.7% vs. 0.1%, 3m annualized) while goods reaccelerated elsewhere — Canada 3.2%, Japan 1.9%, UK 1.8%, Euro area 1.0%.
- US core services slowed to 3.4% (vs. 4.2%); Canada services jumped from low levels to 2.0% (vs. 0.7%), lifted by World Cup-related travel categories.
- Rent inflation eased broadly — Canada 2.0%, UK 3.7%, US 4.3%, Japan 0.5% — edging up only in the Euro area (2.9%).
- Food inflation slowed in Canada, the UK and the Euro area (the latter two now negative) but rose in Japan (2.6%) and the US (3.5%).
- UK stands apart: its 3-month price distribution shifted sharply lower since April on smaller regulated resets and calendar effects, yet trimmed core still ticked up and it was the only economy where core did not surprise to the downside.

### Risks
- The report frames no explicit upside/downside risk scenarios. The main flagged uncertainty is the durability of the energy relief: forecasts were cut on the Strait of Hormuz reopening, leaving the path exposed to any reversal of that agreement.

### Unpacked
June's core prints surprised to the downside almost across the board. **The US decline was broad-based across categories, the Euro area reflected softer-than-expected services, Canada saw slowdowns in nearly all major categories, and Japan was helped in part by falling mobile phone communication fees — only the UK came in line, though its headline surprised slightly lower.** This is the message the aggregate surprise indices confirm: both headline and core have surprised down over the past year everywhere except the Euro area.

The single biggest mover was energy. The US-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz drove 3-month annualized energy inflation down from triple-digit rates to single or low-double digits across the G10. **That shock fed straight into the forecast: [REDACTED] cut 2026 Q4/Q4 headline inflation by 0.4pp in the US, 0.3pp in Canada, 0.1pp in Japan and 0.1pp in the UK, while nudging the Euro area up 0.2pp.**

Beneath the energy swing, the category picture is mixed. US core goods slipped into deflation on a 3-month basis even as goods firmed everywhere else, and US core services cooled meaningfully. Canada is the outlier on services, where the World Cup boosted travel-related categories from a low base. **Rents softened in most economies, a key part of why [REDACTED] still sees US core PCE disinflating.**

Breadth diverges from the averages in a way worth watching. **The distribution of 3-month core rates is skewed higher in the US — large price increases have become more common again after moderating before 2025 — and in the Euro area, while the UK distribution has dropped sharply since April and Canada stays skewed low on soft shelter.** The US is also the only economy where the share of the basket running above 8% keeps grinding higher.

On forecasts, [REDACTED] expects Q4/Q4 core to accelerate into end-2026 in most of the G10 — 2.8% in the UK, 2.6% in the Euro area, 2.5% in Japan, 2.0% in Canada — but to slow in the US to 3.0% core PCE, as shelter disinflation and a fading tariff and software boost offset spillovers from higher energy and commodity prices. The US end-26 core call sits below consensus.

Finally, the harmonized-core lens flags measurement caveats. **On a like-for-like basis, [REDACTED] harmonized core runs notably above the central banks' preferred measures in Canada — where the BoC's statistical measures stripped out World Cup-related upside outliers — and in Japan, but below them in the US and Euro area,** a reminder that headline national core readings are not directly comparable across countries.

subject: G10 Inflation Monitor: Core Inflation Surprises to the Downside Outside of Japan
summary:
# G10 Core Inflation Cools Broadly — Japan the Lone Holdout

**Theme:** December core inflation surprises to the downside almost everywhere; Japan bucks the trend  
**Markets:** G10 core inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Megan Peters, 23 January 2026

### Landscape
- [REDACTED] trimmed core year-over-year sits at +3.0% in the UK, +2.4% in Canada, +2.2% in the US and Euro area, and +1.6% in Japan.
- On a 3-month annualized basis, trimmed core rose in Japan (1.5% vs. 1.0%), the UK (3.2% vs. 2.8%), and the US (1.7% vs. 1.5%), but slowed in the Euro area (1.9% vs. 2.4%) and Canada (1.7% vs. 1.9%).
- December sequential trimmed core ticked up in the UK (3.7% vs. 2.6%), US (2.3% vs. 1.4%, [REDACTED] PCE forecast), Canada (1.2% vs. 0.7%), and Japan (1.1% vs. 1.0%), but fell in the Euro area (1.2% vs. 2.3%).
- Traditional core has fallen ~7pp from peak in the UK, ~5pp in the Euro area and Canada, and ~4pp in the US.
- The share of the basket exceeding an 8% annualized pace held at 11% in the US (vs. 6% in Q1) and remains below 10% elsewhere; the distribution of 3-month rates is close to pre-pandemic norms in most economies.

### Drivers
- Core goods reaccelerated on a 3-month annualized basis in Japan (3.7% vs. 2.1%), the UK (0.8% vs. 0.2%), and Canada (1.6% vs. 1.3%), but slowed in the US (0.2% vs. 1.1%) and the Euro area (-0.6% vs. flat).
- Core services inflation edged up across all developed markets.
- Rent inflation ticked up in the US (1.6% vs. 1.3%), held at 3.3% in the Euro area, and slowed in the UK (3.7% vs. 4.1%), Canada (6.3% vs. 6.4%), and Japan (0.7% vs. 0.8%).
- Energy inflation slowed everywhere except the UK; food inflation rose in most DMs but eased from an elevated pace in Canada.
- Breadth is narrowing: the share of the basket running above 4% on a six-month annualized basis fell in the Euro area, UK, and Japan and was flat in the US and Canada.

### Risks
- Downside to US and UK 2026 core: the forecast slowdown to 2.3% depends on tariff and special policy-related boosts fading — [REDACTED] treats these as fading but does not quantify the risk if they persist.
- Japan is the asymmetric upside outlier: it is the only economy where December core surprised above consensus and where trimmed core accelerated on both monthly and 3-month bases.

### Unpacked
December delivered downside core inflation surprises in the US, UK, Euro area, and Canada, with Japan the sole exception where new core CPI came in a touch above consensus. **The headline read is broad-based cooling outside Japan, though the underlying monthly and 3-month trimmed measures actually firmed in several economies, so the "surprise" is relative to expectations rather than a clean deceleration in the data itself.**

The Euro area stands out as the cleanest disinflation story: sequential trimmed core dropped to 1.2% from 2.3%, the 3-month measure slowed to 1.9%, core goods ran outright negative at -0.6%, and the weighted median monthly rate declined alongside Japan's. **Japan is moving the opposite way — trimmed core rose on every basis, and core goods jumped to 3.7% from 2.1% on a 3-month annualized basis, the fastest goods reacceleration in the group.**

Rent remains the persistent cross-country divide, ranging from 0.7% in Japan to 6.3% in Canada, differences the report notes partly reflect methodology rather than fundamentals alone. [REDACTED] also flags that its harmonized core — which strips a consistent item set across countries — runs below the central banks' preferred measures everywhere except Canada, where excluding owned housing (notably mortgage interest costs) and soft financial services pushes it well above the official read.

**On forecasts, [REDACTED] sees Q4/Q4 year-over-year core slowing to 2.3% by end-2026 in the US and UK, 2.2% in Canada, 1.9% in the Euro area, and 1.4% in Japan — generally below consensus.** Over the past month it nudged up the US and UK end-2026 numbers by 0.1pp each while trimming the Euro area by 0.1pp, with the US and UK slowdowns explicitly tied to fading tariff and policy-related boosts.

subject: G10 Inflation Monitor: Firmer Services, Softer Goods (Peters)
summary:
# G10 Inflation: Goods Cooling, Services Reheating as US Braces for a Tariff-Driven Pickup

**Theme:** Divergent core dynamics — softening goods, firming services, and a US outlier turning up on tariffs  
**Markets:** G10 (DM) core inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 1 June 2025

### Landscape
- [REDACTED] trimmed core (year-over-year) sits at +3.3% in the UK, +3.2% in Canada, +2.4% in the US, +2.3% in the Euro area and +1.7% in Japan.
- April sequential trimmed core (m/m annualized) firmed in the US (+2.5% vs. +2.1%), Japan (+3.1% vs. +1.7%) and Canada (+4.0% vs. +2.8%) but eased in the Euro area (+2.2% vs. +2.8%) and the UK (+1.7% vs. +3.7%).
- On a 3-month annualized basis, trimmed core ticked up in the Euro area (+2.4%), Japan (+2.0%) and Canada (+3.4%) but declined in the US (+2.6%) and the UK (+2.7%).
- The share of the headline basket running above 4% (6-month annualized) rose for a sixth straight month in the UK to 62%, and edged up in the Euro area to 23%, but fell in the US (23% vs. 34%) and Canada (34% vs. 41%) and held at 36% in Japan.
- Traditional core has fallen from its cyclical peak by 5.2pp (UK), 4.2pp (US PCE and Canada) and 3.8pp (Euro area) on a 3-month average annualized basis, but only 2.6pp in Japan.

### Drivers
- Core goods disinflation is broadening across DMs (3-month annualized), led by Japan (-1.7pp to +5.8%) and the UK (-1.0pp to -0.9%).
- Core services are reaccelerating outside the US and Japan, rising in Canada (+3.2pp to +6.4%), the UK (+2.4pp to +7.6%) and the Euro area (+1.8pp to +5.3%), while the US eased (-0.9pp to +3.1%).

- Energy remains a swing factor: Canada fell sharply (-42.7%) on removal of the consumer carbon tax, the Euro area turned negative (-15.1%), while Japan (+6.8%) and the UK (+3.4%) rose as price-control measures ended.
- The distribution of 3-month inflation rates keeps shifting back toward pre-pandemic norms, most clearly in the US and Euro area, and extreme moves (above 8% annualized) are contained except in the UK (15%) and Japan (19%).

### Risks
- Upside, US: [REDACTED] sees year-over-year core climbing to +3.6% by end-2025 on tariff-driven price pressures — the one DM where the forecast rises rather than falls.
- Upside, Europe: [REDACTED] revised up end-2025 core by 0.3pp (Euro area) and 0.2pp (UK), citing a smaller disinflationary impulse from trade diversion after US-China de-escalation.
- Upside, Canada: April core surprised high with a composition [REDACTED] reads as reflecting retaliatory tariffs.
- The skew is asymmetric to the upside — the flagged surprises and forecast revisions all point higher, with no comparable downside scenario named.

### Unpacked
The central split this month is between goods and services. **Core goods inflation is cooling across every DM on a 3-month basis, while core services are firming everywhere except the US and Japan** — a mirror image of the US, where services led April's sequential softening even as its headline trimmed core firmed. That US firming is the near-term noise; the structural signal [REDACTED] emphasizes is that the US is the sole G10 economy where the year-end core forecast points up.

Underneath the services move, rent is the most country-specific line. **Canada's rent inflation more than doubled to +5.1% (3-month annualized), the sharpest acceleration in the group**, while the US held flat at +3.9% and the UK cooled. [REDACTED] notes cross-country rent comparisons are partly a measurement artifact, so the divergence overstates true differences in tenant costs.

Energy and food explain much of the remaining cross-country noise, and several moves trace to policy rather than markets. **Canada's -42.7% energy print reflects the removal of the consumer carbon tax, while Japan's and the UK's energy upticks follow the end of electricity and gas price controls** — base effects that will wash through rather than signal underlying pressure. Food slowed in the US, UK and Japan but rose in Canada and the Euro area.

The April surprises cluster on the upside and each has a distinct cause. **The UK's core beat came from regulated and volatile components, the Euro area's from Easter timing distortions, and Canada's from a composition consistent with retaliatory tariffs** — idiosyncratic drivers rather than a common reflation, but all pushing the same direction.

On forecasts, [REDACTED] expects year-over-year core to end 2025 at +3.6% in the US, then decline to +3.1% (UK), +2.2% (Canada), +2.1% (Euro area) and +1.5% (Japan). **These end-2025 calls sit below consensus everywhere except the US**, where tariffs drive the above-consensus view. The recent upward revisions in the Euro area, UK and US were tied to a weaker disinflationary pull from trade diversion after the US-China thaw.

Finally, the harmonized-core work reframes several headline reads. **On a like-for-like basis, [REDACTED] harmonized core runs materially below the central banks' preferred measures in the US, Canada and Japan** — in the US because owned housing (absent from Euro-area and UK baskets) is stripped out, in Canada because the firm financial-services category is removed, and in Japan because hot food-away-from-home and alcohol are excluded. The practical takeaway is that some of the apparent US and Canadian firmness reflects basket construction, not broader underlying pressure.

summary:
# Market Stress Benign, With Only a Marginal Uptick From Very Low Levels

**Theme:** Market function and microstructure across asset classes  
**Markets:** Global cross-asset (DM credit, rates, equities, EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], William Marshall, 6 July 2026  

### Landscape
- Broad market-stress measures have deteriorated very slightly over the past month but remain very benign versus historic norms, as of the 3 July snapshot.
- Rates microstructure has improved after a brief drop in market depth in April and May, with yield sensitivity to orderflow declining again.
- Funding costs have continued to ease, supporting wider swap spreads.
- Sovereign spreads have widened slightly from conflict-driven tights.
- Equity bid-ask spreads have moved broadly sideways in the US and Europe over the month; UK spreads have widened slightly from their tights.
- Equity funding spreads have reversed part of their recent widening but stay elevated on a longer lookback.

### Drivers
- Easing funding costs are the main supportive force in rates, feeding through to wider swap spreads.
- Recovering rates market depth has pulled yield sensitivity to orderflow back down after the spring dip.
- A modest widening in sovereign spreads reflects normalization away from conflict-tights rather than fresh stress.
- Equity funding pressure is partially unwinding but remains high relative to its longer history — a mixed signal rather than a clean improvement.

### Unpacked
**The overall message is one of calm: the aggregate stress index sits at very low levels by historical standards, and the small month-on-month deterioration does not change that picture.** The report constructs its indices by normalizing stress indicators within each market segment against full-sample averages, averaging across indicators in a category, and then averaging categories into an aggregate, all shown as 3-day moving averages with levels as of 3 July.

**In rates, the story is one of repair after a spring wobble.** Market depth dropped briefly in April and May, but microstructure measures have since improved and the sensitivity of yields to orderflow has fallen again. Alongside this, funding costs have kept easing, which has supported a widening in swap spreads, while sovereign spreads have edged wider from levels compressed during the earlier conflict episode.

**In equities, the picture is flatter and more mixed.** Bid-ask spreads have been broadly sideways in the US and Europe over the past month, with only the UK showing a slight widening from its tights. Equity funding spreads have given back part of their recent widening but remain elevated when viewed over a longer window, leaving that one measure as the notable outlier against an otherwise benign backdrop.

The note is a monitor built around charts and normalized indices rather than a trade recommendation, and it offers no explicit trade idea.

- Aggregate market stress measures are little changed or incrementally improved versus a month ago, with levels reported as of June 5.

subject: Global Markets Comment: Market Stress Monitor — 30 March 2026
summary:
# US Treasury Liquidity Thins, but Funding Markets Hold

**Theme:** Market microstructure softening without a funding-stress signal  
**Markets:** US Treasuries, DM credit, rates, equities and EM  
**Source:** [REDACTED], William Marshall, 30 March 2026

### Landscape
- US Treasury market depth declined last week, pointing to thinner liquidity as of the March 27 close.
- Estimated cost-to-sweep and price sensitivity to flows both rose, consistent with worse market function since the onset of the conflict.
- The deterioration in microstructure measures has been smaller than in recent stress events.
- Secured USD funding costs have been stable, showing no strain in dollar funding.
- Term cross-currency bases widened from tight levels.

### Drivers
- Thinning Treasury liquidity is being driven by a more uncertain and volatile macro backdrop; the current shifts echo those seen when hike risk came into focus in 2022.
- Wider cross-currency bases reflect a generalized rise in risk premia and positioning rather than genuine difficulty sourcing dollars — funding channels remain functional.

### Unpacked
The report is a scoreboard of market-function measures across DM credit, rates, equities and EM, normalized by segment and averaged into category and aggregate stress indices shown as three-day moving averages. The substantive read sits in the intro; the body is exhibit-driven.

**The core message is that market microstructure has softened but funding has not.** Treasury depth fell, and cost-to-sweep and price sensitivity to flows rose — all signs of thinner liquidity and some worsening in function since the conflict began. The scale of these moves, though, is smaller than in recent stress episodes, and their pattern matches the 2022 experience as rate-hike risk came into view, framing the shift as a normal response to a more volatile macro environment rather than an acute break.

**Funding markets tell a calmer story.** Secured USD funding costs have held steady, and while term cross-currency bases widened from tight levels, that is read as a broad increase in risk premia and behavior rather than a material dollar-funding problem at this point. The note flags no explicit trade idea and does not lay out a distinct risk scenario beyond this baseline.

# Foreign Official Selling Drives December Outflows from Long-Term US Treasuries

**Theme:** December TIC flows — foreign net buying of US securities overall, but official-sector selling of long-term Treasuries  
**Markets:** US cross-border securities flows  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Lexi Kanter, 18 February 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Foreign investors net purchased long-term US securities overall in December, on valuation-adjusted estimates from preliminary US Treasury data.
- Within that total, foreign investors net sold long-term US Treasuries, while net buying corporate bonds, equities and agency securities.
- Buying of corporate bonds, equities and agency securities came from private investors; the outflow from long-term Treasuries was driven by official investors.
- Canada was the largest net buyer of long-term Treasuries, followed by France.
- The United Kingdom swung to the largest net seller in December, having been the largest net buyer in November.
- Brazil was the second-largest net seller, linked primarily to over $20bn of central bank spot FX intervention.
- At the regional level, Europe, Latin America and Asia were all net sellers.

### At issue
The US Treasury released preliminary December TIC (Treasury International Capital) data on cross-border securities flows. On a valuation-adjusted basis, foreign investors were net buyers of long-term US securities in the month, but the composition split by sector and by investor type: private buying of corporate bonds, equities and agencies against official-sector selling of long-term Treasuries. Country detail shows the UK moving from top buyer to top seller month-over-month, and Brazil among the largest sellers on the back of central bank FX intervention exceeding $20bn.

- Fluxos líquidos para fundos globais de ações viraram negativos: -US$9bi na semana até 26 de março, ante +US$43bi na semana anterior.

**Markets:** Global cross-border fund flows (equities, fixed income, FX)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 24 January 2025  

### Landscape
- Global equity funds took in +$6bn in the week ending January 22, down from +$13bn the prior week.
- Global fixed income funds held firm at +$14bn, up from +$11bn the previous week.
- Money market fund assets rose $62bn on the week.
- Within G10 equities, US led inflows, followed by Japan and Western Europe ex. UK.
- Global EM equity benchmarks and mainland China equity funds both saw net outflows.
- EM fixed income flows were negative across both hard-currency and local-currency bond funds.
- Industrials drew the largest sector equity inflows; other sector funds were muted.

### Drivers
- Equity inflows are decelerating for a second week, with the slowdown broad rather than concentrated in one region.
- Foreign demand for US equities has risen more than domestic demand as a percentage of AUM in recent weeks — the report's flagged focus (Chart of the Week).
- Fixed income demand is firming, led by municipal bond funds and sustained inflows into bank loan, government, and Agg-type funds.
- EM demand is weak on both sides of the book, with equity and bond flows turning negative.
- Cross-border FX flows show persistent demand for USD.

### Unpacked
**The headline is a cooling equity bid alongside steady demand for bonds and dollars — a rotation in tone rather than a reversal.** Equity inflows more than halved week-on-week to +$6bn, but fixed income flows and money market accumulation both strengthened, leaving the overall picture one of caution rather than risk-off.

Sector positioning offered little to read into beyond industrials, which took the largest net inflows while other sector funds stayed muted. On the currency side, cross-border flows continued to favor the USD.

# July GSAI Jumps to 64.6 as New Orders Surge, but Price Pressures Cool Off the Peak

**Theme:** Activity accelerating on stronger orders while price components retreat from June highs  
**Markets:** US business activity / manufacturing and services  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 31 July 2026

### Landscape
- The headline GSAI rose 3.1pt to 64.6 in July, with above-50 signaling above-trend growth in the analyst read of activity.
- New orders jumped 6.7pt to 69.4 and shipments rose 4.5pt to 64.6, while employment fell 3.7pt to 44.8.
- The exports component dropped 15.0pt to 60.0, partly retracing June's spike; inventories rose 2.1pt to 60.1, lifting the orders-less-inventories gap 9.3pt to +4.6.
- Price components eased: output prices fell 13.0pt to 80.8 (off June's record high), materials prices fell 6.3pt to 75.0, and wages edged down 0.3pt to 71.9.
- [REDACTED] survey trackers for both manufacturing (+1.6pt to 55.8) and services (+1.6pt to 54.5) rose, as did their employment sub-components (manufacturing 51.5, services 51.1).

### Drivers
- Demand is the main force lifting the index, with new orders and shipments both climbing and the orders-less-inventories gap turning positive — a signal of continued forward momentum.
- Price pressure is cooling from an extreme peak but remains high in level; output, materials, and wage components all fell yet still sit well above 50, so disinflation is directional rather than complete.
- Labor demand in the GSAI softened (employment 44.8), diverging from the [REDACTED] survey trackers where manufacturing and services employment both firmed — a mixed signal on hiring.
- Commodity-cost pass-through is an active theme: 76% of surveyed analysts expect higher oil and commodity prices to raise input costs and 92% expect covered companies to raise their own prices, essentially unchanged from March.

### Risks
- Downside: 59% of surveyed analysts expect higher gasoline and other prices to weigh on demand in their sector over the next six months, though this is below the 69% share in March, suggesting the analyst-perceived demand drag has eased somewhat.
- Downside on margins: in the Kansas City Fed surveys, roughly 60% of firms reported margins decreasing since the start of the year versus about a quarter reporting increases.
- Offsetting upside: roughly half of KC Fed firms expect higher demand over the rest of the year, against about a third expecting lower and a third expecting flat.

### Unpacked
The July print reads as a genuine pickup in activity rather than a price artifact. **Some of the strength in survey levels reflects nominal bias — respondents thinking in dollar rather than real terms — but the price-adjusted trackers still look solid after correcting for it.** That distinction matters this month precisely because the price components, while falling, remain elevated enough to inflate raw index levels.

**The composition is the story: orders and shipments carried the index higher even as employment fell and the price components rolled over from June's extremes.** Output prices had set a survey record in June before dropping 13pt, and materials prices came off their high as well, so the cost impulse is fading from a peak rather than collapsing. The sharp reversal in exports mostly undoes June's outsized jump rather than signaling a new trend.

The special questions frame the cost dynamic that analysts continue to watch. The commodity-cost view is remarkably stable versus March — near-universal expectation that companies pass higher input costs into their own prices — while the share seeing energy prices as a demand drag has narrowed. **The net picture from the firm-level surveys is squeezed margins so far this year paired with more optimism about demand ahead**, a combination consistent with an economy where activity is firming but pricing power and cost pressures are still being negotiated.

subject: US Daily: February GSAI: No Leap This Year (Rindels)
summary:
# US Activity Cools: GSAI Drops Below Trend as Policy Uncertainty Bites

**Theme:** Broad-based softening in business activity alongside elevated but not yet paralyzing policy uncertainty  
**Markets:** US business activity and inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 28 February 2025  

### Landscape
- Headline GSAI fell 9.8pt to 50.4 in February — barely above the 50 mark that [REDACTED] reads as consistent with trend growth rather than no growth.
- New orders dropped 24.2pt to 43.5 and shipments fell 14.7pt to 46.4, both deep in contraction.
- Employment component eased 3.8pt to 47.2; exports flat at 43.8; inventories rose 8.9pt to 58.9, pushing the orders-less-inventories gap down 33.1pt to -15.4.
- On prices, materials prices rose 6.7pt to 69.2 and wages rose 5.8pt to 67.6, while output prices fell 6.8pt to 54.2.
- [REDACTED] manufacturing survey tracker slipped 1.3pt to 52.2 and the nonmanufacturing tracker fell 0.9pt to 53.2; employment sub-components sat just in contraction (manufacturing 49.6, services 49.8).

### Drivers
- Demand is weakening fast: the collapse in new orders and shipments, paired with rising inventories, points to firms carrying more stock against softening order flow.
- Cost pressure is building on inputs even as final pricing softens — materials and wages components rose while output prices fell, squeezing margins.
- Policy uncertainty is now the dominant overhang: all but one surveyed [REDACTED] analyst reported elevated uncertainty in their sector, driven mainly by tariffs, immigration policy, and potential regulatory change.
- Immigration reliance is rising and at risk: Dallas Fed firms reporting use of immigrant workers jumped to 33% (manufacturing) and 21% (services) from 20% and 12% a year earlier, with a quarter of manufacturers expecting policy changes to hinder hiring and retention.
- Inflation expectations are drifting lower on net: Philadelphia Fed firms reported moderating price inflation over the past year and expected further slowing in 2025, with services firms' year-ahead price expectations down 0.8pp to 2.0%.

### Risks
- Upside to prices (analyst view): tariffs are widely expected to raise input costs, and many firms indicated they would pass these through — though some flagged that diminished pricing power would limit their ability to do so.
- Downside to demand (analyst view): trade policy uncertainty is already reported to be hindering demand, with clients delaying purchases or shortening contracts.
- Contained investment risk (analyst view): despite elevated uncertainty, 75% of [REDACTED] analysts did not expect firms to delay or cancel investment; the remaining 25% expected delay but not cancellation — a notably limited hit to capex.

### Unpacked
**The February GSAI reading is weak beneath the headline: at 50.4 it sits barely in expansion, but its composition is clearly contractionary.** The steep falls in new orders and shipments are the standout, and the simultaneous jump in inventories drove the orders-less-inventories gap sharply negative — a configuration that typically signals demand cooling faster than firms had planned for. Other [REDACTED] survey trackers echo the softening, with both manufacturing and nonmanufacturing indices lower and their employment sub-components sitting just below 50.

The price signals cut both ways. **Input costs are still climbing — materials prices and wages both rose — while output prices fell, pointing to margin pressure rather than accelerating final-goods inflation.** The Philadelphia Fed special questions reinforce the disinflationary read on final prices: manufacturing firms reported unchanged price inflation over the prior four quarters at +3.0% and services firms reported none at all, down from +0.5% in November. Year-ahead price expectations held at +3.0% for manufacturers but fell to +2.0% for services. Wage expectations diverged, rising to +3.9% for manufacturers but falling to +3.0% for services.

The Dallas Fed data document a rising and increasingly exposed dependence on immigrant labor. **Reliance on workers who moved from another country climbed sharply over the year, and firms anticipating tighter immigration policy said they are turning to automation, AI, and higher worker utilization to cope.** Among firms already using immigrant workers, 43% of manufacturers and 24% of services firms said that reliance had increased, against just 4.3% reporting a decrease.

On trade, the Dallas Fed responses lay out a spectrum. **Firms broadly expect tariffs to raise input costs, but their pricing response varies — some will pass costs through, others only if tariffs persist or margins require it, and some lack the pricing power to do so at all.** A few reported being unable to find alternatives to tariff-exposed inputs; some had front-loaded imports or built inventory ahead of tariffs; and some noted clients holding off on purchases or shortening contracts. Firms that are US-based or already domestically sourced expected tariffs to help them.

**The GSAI special questions paint uncertainty as pervasive but not yet decisive for investment.** Nearly every analyst reported elevated uncertainty — centered on tariffs, immigration, and regulation — yet three-quarters did not expect firms to delay or cancel investment, and the rest expected delay only. Beyond capex, analysts flagged that firms may respond by raising prices or by increasing domestic manufacturing and sourcing.

subject: US Daily: April GSAI: Not Quite a Spring (Rindels)
summary:
# April GSAI Ticks Up but Composition Weakens as Trade-War Fears Spread to Layoffs

**Theme:** A modest headline rebound masks falling employment and orders, with analysts and firms flagging tariff-driven production disruptions  
**Markets:** US business activity and inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 30 April 2025

### Definitive impacts
- Headline GSAI rose +3.6pt to 44.5 in April, partially reversing a ~20pt cumulative drop across February and March.
- Employment component fell -20.5pt to 33.5, its lowest since October 2023; new orders declined -1.2pt to 32.2, so the gain was carried by shipments (+4.5pt to 40.6).
- Inventories surged +37.4pt to 62.0 after March's lowest reading since January 2010; the orders-less-inventories gap dropped -38.6pt to -29.8, and exports fell -11.1pt to 55.6.
- Price components rose — materials prices +21.5pt to 78.6 and output prices +4.9pt to 66.2 — while wages fell -5.7pt to 57.9.
- [REDACTED] manufacturing survey tracker fell -3.6pt to 46.9 (lowest since June 2023) and the nonmanufacturing tracker -1.3pt to 49.2 (lowest since May 2020); their employment sub-components also fell (manufacturing 47.2, services 48.3).
- In the GSAI special questions, ~45% of analysts flagged future retaliatory tariffs as a production-disruption risk, 30% cited input-cost-driven loss of price competitiveness, and 20% cited China's rare-earth export restrictions; 65% said their industries are already adapting.
- In the Dallas Fed special questions, 80% of manufacturing and 63% of services firms expected tariffs to raise input costs; 20% of manufacturers and 15% of services firms expected profit margins to fall significantly; ~30% expected lower employment while ~65% expected no employment impact.
- Among firms passing tariff costs on, 25% expected to pass the full cost, 30% most, and 44% some; 17% expected immediate pass-through and 31% within a month. Roughly half reported absorbing costs internally.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] characterizes April's composition as "weak on net" despite the headline rise, reading the employment collapse and order weakness as the more meaningful signals.
- [REDACTED] treats the analyst survey as "concerning," inferring that risks from further escalation around the paused reciprocal tariffs are serious given that retaliatory tariffs were the most-cited disruption channel.
- [REDACTED] flags rare-earth restrictions as potentially reducing chip availability, which analysts see as particularly disruptive for hardware and semiconductor coverage.

### Backdrop
The GSAI is [REDACTED]'s monthly diffusion index built from its own analysts' reads on the industries they cover, weighted 30% new orders, 25% shipments, 20% employment, 15% materials prices, and 10% inventories — mirroring the ISM's pre-2008 method but substituting materials prices for supplier deliveries. It spans services and manufacturing. As with ISM, 50 nominally separates growth from contraction, though [REDACTED] notes a reading of 50 aligns better with trend growth than with no growth, so sub-50 prints signal below-trend activity. April responses were collected 22–25 April.

### At issue
This is the April 2025 GSAI release, paired with two sets of special questions. [REDACTED] asked its analysts how three trade-war channels — loss of price competitiveness from higher input costs, prohibitive retaliatory tariffs on exports, and loss of access to rare earth elements — would hit the companies they cover; roughly half expected production disruptions and layoffs. Separately, the note draws on the Dallas Fed manufacturing and services surveys, whose own special questions probed how firms expect tariffs to affect costs, prices, margins, employment, and cost pass-through.

### Unpacked
The title's "not quite a spring" captures the tension in the print: the headline moved up, but almost every forward-looking internal told the opposite story. **The rebound was mechanical rather than broad — shipments and a inventory snapback lifted the index while the demand and labor signals that matter more for the trajectory deteriorated.** The employment drop to its lowest since October 2023 is the standout, and it lines up with softening employment components across [REDACTED]'s other survey trackers.

The inventory surge alongside falling new orders and exports is worth sitting with. **A collapsing orders-less-inventories gap points to firms building stock into weakening demand — consistent with frontloading purchases ahead of tariffs rather than genuine strength.** Firms in the Dallas Fed survey confirmed this behavior directly, alongside finding new domestic suppliers.

The two survey layers reinforce each other on prices. **Tariffs are showing up as a cost-and-price story now and a margin-and-jobs story later:** materials prices jumped, most firms expect higher input and selling prices, and a large share are already passing costs to customers — many immediately or within a month — while a meaningful minority expect significant margin compression.

On the labor question the two sources diverge in a telling way. [REDACTED]'s analysts, looking across whole industries, see roughly half at risk of disruption and layoffs, whereas individual Dallas Fed firms mostly expected no employment impact. **The gap suggests the layoff risk is concentrated and contingent on escalation rather than already baked in** — retaliatory tariffs, the top-cited channel, are tied to the paused reciprocal tariffs that could still snap back. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

# US Jobless Claims: A Thanksgiving-Distorted Plunge, Not a Genuine Labor-Market Improvement

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US weekly jobless claims  
**General comment:** Cautionary read of a strong print — treats the drop as a seasonal artifact rather than a signal, against a naïve take of the headline.

### Context
Initial jobless claims for the week ended November 29 came in at 191k, far below the 220k median forecast and well under [REDACTED]'s own 215k estimate, with continuing claims also a touch below consensus. The comment addresses how much of that surprise reflects real labor-market strength versus a statistical quirk around the Thanksgiving holiday.

### The case
- **The sharp fall is largely a seasonal-adjustment artifact, not a genuine improvement.** Initial claims dropped 27k to 191k, but the seasonal factor mis-sized the holiday effect. On a non-seasonally-adjusted basis, claims fell 49k this year — close to the ~45k typical of prior Thanksgiving weeks with a similar calendar layout — yet the seasonal factor only anticipated a 22k decline. That gap between the expected and actual raw drop is what mechanically pushed the adjusted headline so low, rather than a fresh wave of stronger hiring or fewer layoffs.
- **The underlying picture is steady, not improving.** State-level detail is unremarkable: claims fell 8k in California and 2k each in New York, Washington and Texas, and rose 2k in Pennsylvania. Continuing claims — those still drawing benefits — declined only 4k to 1,939k, modestly below consensus but consistent with a labor market that is holding roughly flat rather than accelerating.

### Implications
- The headline overstates labor-market strength; the "true" signal is closer to unchanged, as reflected in the small US MAP adjustments (a -2pt correction to initial claims for Thanksgiving volatility).
- The distortion is expected to unwind, so readers should discount this print and watch subsequent weeks for the cleaner trend rather than extrapolate the 191k figure.

# EUA: pedidos iniciais de seguro-desemprego caem ao menor nível desde 1969, mas o próprio dado alerta para ruído sazonal

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** Dados semanais de seguro-desemprego nos EUA  
**General comment:** Leitura de superfície forte, mas o comentário é deliberadamente cauteloso — trata o número como distorcido por sazonalidade, não como sinal de fortalecimento do mercado de trabalho.

### Contexto
Os pedidos iniciais de seguro-desemprego da semana encerrada em 18 de julho vieram muito abaixo do esperado. O comentário avalia o que essa queda expressiva de fato significa para a leitura do mercado de trabalho.

### Os argumentos
- **A queda foi grande e ampla, mas o nível absoluto é o ponto de atenção.** Os pedidos iniciais recuaram 22 mil, para 187 mil, contra estimativa [REDACTED] de 205 mil e mediana de 210 mil — o menor patamar desde 1969. A média móvel de quatro semanas caiu 7 mil, para 208 mil, e as quedas estaduais foram disseminadas (‑4 mil no Texas; ‑3 mil em Michigan e Nova York; ‑2 mil em Illinois e Tennessee), com alta apenas em Massachusetts (+2 mil). Os pedidos continuados também recuaram, 2 mil para 1.796 mil, levemente abaixo do esperado.
- **O número deve ser lido com desconto por fatores sazonais, não como melhora real.** Os pedidos iniciais ajustados sazonalmente caíram entre junho e julho nos últimos dois anos, e as leituras de julho tendem a ser mais voláteis. Por isso, a expectativa é de rebote parcial dos pedidos na semana seguinte — ou seja, parte da queda é atribuída a ruído sazonal, e não a um enfraquecimento das demissões.

### Implicações
- O dado surpreende para baixo nos pedidos, mas o próprio comentário desencoraja extrapolar força do mercado de trabalho a partir dele.
- O rebote esperado na próxima leitura é o teste: a interpretação sazonal só se confirma se os pedidos voltarem a subir.

# US Consumer: Resilient Spending Meets an Energy-Driven Income Squeeze

**Theme:** Higher energy prices erode real income and confidence even as balance sheets hold up  
**Markets:** US consumer / household economy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Joseph Briggs, 30 April 2026

### Landscape
- Real PCE growth tracking a healthy 2.1% y/y through March; March headline retail sales rose 1.7% m/m (with upward revisions), core up 0.7% nominal / 0.6% real.
- Payrolls rose 178k in March, but the three-month average (+68k) and estimated underlying pace (+53k) were softer; unemployment ticked down 0.1pp to 4.3%.
- Real disposable income growth slowed 0.8pp to 0.4% y/y (and 0.3pp to 0.2% on a 6-month annualized basis) in March.
- Net worth-to-disposable-income ratio near its all-time high after the equity rebound; saving rate fell 0.3pp to 3.6% in March.
- Consumer credit growth up 0.2pp to 2.3% y/y (2.6% 6-month annualized) in February; home equity loans running at +4.5% (12-week annualized through April 15).
- UMich sentiment fell 3.5pt to 49.8, its lowest on record; Conference Board confidence edged up 0.6pt to 92.8.

### Drivers
- **Energy prices are the dominant new drag**, lifting headline inflation and eroding spending power, with the heaviest hit on lower-income households that spend more of their budget on energy — the reason 2026 real PCE is cut to a below-consensus 1.3% Q4/Q4 (from 2.1% in 2025).
- **Labor market has stabilized but is set to slow**; the March gain was flattered by better weather and the end of strikes, and growth headwinds from the war in Iran are expected to cut job growth to 31k/month for the rest of 2026, pushing unemployment to 4.6% by year-end.
- **A fiscal tailwind is being neutralized**: the OBBBA's higher refunds and lower tax payments should add $75–90bn to household income in 2026, but higher capital gains tax payments have largely offset it.
- **Precautionary saving is building**, with the saving rate forecast to rise to 4.1% by end-2026 and 4.7% by end-2027 on labor-market and geopolitical concerns — a force that diverts income from spending.
- **Sentiment is deteriorating in real time**; daily Morning Consult data show continued declines since the start of the war in Iran, a leading signal to watch against the more mixed official surveys.

### Risks
- **Downside (labor market):** the analyst sees risks skewed toward more labor-market weakening if higher energy prices drag harder on growth or AI-related job losses run larger than expected.
- **Downside (credit quality):** although aggregate leverage and debt-servicing costs are low, 90+ day credit card and subprime auto delinquencies remain elevated versus history.

### Unpacked
The through-line is a consumer entering 2026 on solid footing but facing a fresh, energy-driven squeeze on real incomes. **Spending has held up — real PCE at 2.1% y/y and a strong March retail print — but the forecast now calls for a marked deceleration to 1.3% real PCE growth on a Q4/Q4 basis, below consensus, as energy-led inflation eats into purchasing power.** The strength on display is largely backward-looking; the headwind is what shapes the rest of the year.

On the labor side, the March payroll gain of 178k overstates momentum. **Stripping out weather and the end of strikes, the underlying pace is closer to 53k, and job growth is expected to fall to about 31k/month with unemployment drifting up to 4.6% by end-2026.** The read here is stabilization, not recovery, with the balance of risks tilted toward further softening.

Income is where the report concentrates its concern. **The OBBBA's $75–90bn boost to household income has been offset on net by higher capital gains tax payments, leaving energy-driven inflation to do the damage — real income growth is cut to 1.3% for 2026, and just 0.6% for the bottom income quintile.** The distributional point matters: lower-income households carry a larger energy share and absorb a disproportionate share of the hit.

Balance sheets remain the offsetting strength. **Net worth relative to income sits near record highs after the equity rebound, and while the saving rate dipped to 3.6% in March, it is projected to rise toward 4.1% by end-2026 and 4.7% by end-2027 as precautionary motives build.** Debt levels are benign in aggregate, but the elevated credit card and subprime auto delinquencies are a pocket of stress beneath the calm headline.

Confidence data are sending a starker signal than the hard data. **UMich sentiment hit a record low of 49.8 even as the Conference Board measure nudged higher, and higher-frequency Morning Consult data confirm the slide dates to the start of the war in Iran** — geopolitics and energy prices feeding directly into how households feel about their prospects. The report offers no explicit trade idea; it is a state-of-play dashboard rather than a positioning call.
